investors.exclusions: We want companies where the customers pay for using the product or service directly. In other words, “I deliver value to you, you pay me.” We don’t like three-way business models as at the stage we invest it’s impossible to tell a company will become the next Google or Facebook. As a corollary, we don’t invest in companies built on media, content, advertising. We typically only consider companies where the founding team is located in the San Francisco Bay Area. This is not a function of where K9 is located, but because we believe that there is something that happens in Silicon Valley, which cannot be easily replicated in other geographies. We welcome working with remote or distributed teams (a change in our thinking), but absolutely will not consider companies that plan to outsource the development of their core technology/product.

articles.title: Fabric molds could bring material-saving concrete beams within reach
articles.description: MIT engineers cast a concrete beam using a sewn fabric mold with one-third the amount of concrete and half as much steel as a conventional beam.

articles.title: How to predict the behavior of molecules from scant data
articles.description: A machine-learning approach called CheMeleon provides a practical way to develop new drugs or other molecules with much less detailed, expensive experimentation.

articles.title: MIT affiliates elected 2026 American Geophysical Union Fellows
articles.description: Anthea Coster, Carolyn Ruppel, César Terrer, and eight additional alumni are honored for their work in the geosciences.

articles.title: Scene at MIT: Beautiful, intricate, creative quilts
articles.description: The MIT Quilt Show, featuring more than 40 quilted projects from 20 members of the MIT community, drew almost 1,000 visitors over three days.

articles.title: Studying bacteria and the cells they infect
articles.description: By exploring how bacteria hijack cell functions, Associate Professor Rebecca Lamason hopes to learn more about how host cells carry out those functions.

articles.title: Pinning down the structure of quark-gluon plasma, the universe’s first fluid
articles.description: A new method picks up where Einstein left off, to predict how particles move through fluid under extreme conditions.

articles.title: Clearing up a robot’s fuzzy memory
articles.description: A new system identifies and corrects unreliable object descriptions stored in a robot’s memory, improving the robot’s ability to interact with its environment.

articles.title: Mentees, colleagues, friends share remembrances of Susumu Tonegawa
articles.description: To remember the longtime professor, lab members, alumni, colleagues, and other well-wishers gathered with members of his family in MIT Building 46 and online.

articles.title: MIT-led team receives funding to develop a wearable monitor for early disease detection
articles.description: Awarded up to $38 million from ARPA-H, the team aims to create a low-power, noninvasive sensor patch that measures heart failure and sepsis biomarkers in real-time.

articles.title: Dream, build, destroy, repeat
articles.description: Members of the student-run MIT Combat Robotics Club learn through destruction.

articles.title: 3 Questions: Building more resilient minerals supply chains
articles.description: Elsa Olivetti, co-director of the MIT Minerals Stewardship Consortium, discusses how research and collaborations can strengthen mineral supply chains.

articles.title: Featured video: Changing the conversation about endometriosis
articles.description: Documentary shines a powerful light on a painful disease that affects 265 million women, highlights efforts at MIT’s Center for Gynepathology Research to study the disease and find treatments.

articles.title: Building connections across the research infrastructure
articles.description: MIT.nano and the Northeast Microelectronics Coalition gathered facility leaders and technology professionals from across the nation to explore ways to make shared-access facilities more connected.

articles.title: Lemelson-MIT brings invention education to classrooms from kindergarten to college
articles.description: A new initiative in California, Tennessee, and New England puts learning by doing at the center of students’ STEM pathways, in step with MIT for America’s focus on helping students design, make, and innovate.

articles.title: Faces of MIT: Vera Grbic
articles.description: IDHR communications officer Vera Grbic helps connect the MIT community with resources, support, and information through clear and accessible messaging.

articles.title: Powering up for a pivotal moment
articles.description: From a nuclear revival to qubits, the MIT Energy Initiative’s annual research conference tracked deployment of today’s technologies to discovery of tomorrow’s breakthroughs.

articles.title: A flexible new route to designer materials built from nanoparticles
articles.description: Pliable connector molecules could be key to creating nanoparticle-based materials for photonics, chemical catalysis, medicine, and more.

articles.title: Regina Barzilay and Jim Collins win Pritzker Prize for AI and Science Research Excellence for work in AI-enabled antibiotic discovery
articles.description: The MIT professors collaborated to identify the first AI-discovered antibiotic, a scientific breakthrough that is widely recognized as a milestone in AI-driven drug discovery.

articles.title: MIT in the media: “Unpack My Cambridge" with President Sally Kornbluth
articles.description: Kornbluth: “We hope to see you here soon on a visit to MIT, whether you are a prospective student, whether you are a tourist or whether you are just someone who likes really cool things.”

articles.title: MIT engineers design a safer, more efficient vaccination system for farmed fish
articles.description: Water-resistant microneedles made from food-grade silk could deliver vaccines to help prevent the spread of disease in aquaculture.

articles.title: MIT affiliates named 2026 Schmidt Sciences AI2050 Fellows
articles.description: Five MIT faculty members and two additional alumni are honored with fellowships to advance research on beneficial AI.

articles.title: J-PAL North America launches ARTEMIS to train early-career researchers
articles.description: The Applied Research Training in Evaluation, Methods, and Impact Studies program provides dedicated support to help researchers overcome barriers to pursue and obtain funding for randomized evaluations.

articles.title: Study pinpoints states with steepest warming trends since 1980
articles.description: The findings indicate where adaptive measures are needed most around the United States.

articles.title: Q&A: Hey AI, who should I vote for this year?
articles.description: MIT professors Adam Berinsky and Chara Podimata discuss a new project to track how AI chatbots are responding to questions about the 2026 U.S. midterm elections.

articles.title: MIT engineers create nanoparticles for delivering personalized cancer vaccines
articles.description: The particles carry a customized dose of cancer antigens that can provoke a strong immune response against tumors.

articles.title: Next Haunt: A scary “problem set” in the basement of Next House
articles.description: For more than a decade, MIT students have turned Next House’s basement into a spooky escape-room style test of puzzles, teamwork, and ingenuity.

articles.title: Magnetic sensors track muscle movement, for better prosthetic limb control
articles.description: Researchers hope to use these sensors to help people with amputation achieve more natural movements with their prosthetic limbs.

articles.title: New system gives users more control over their online experience
articles.description: The Social.Wiki framework enables anyone to easily edit social websites within the system, while allowing them to choose the content they see.

articles.title: Capturing the complete process of embryonic development
articles.description: By tracking over 1 million cells, researchers created a detailed map of embryonic development in mice. It could provide development and disease insights.

articles.title: Seven MIT affiliates elected to the National Academy of Medicine for 2026
articles.description: Professor Michael Yaffe and six MIT alumni are honored for their outstanding professional achievement and commitment to service.

articles.title: How the biggest Alzheimer’s risk gene disrupts the process of insulating neurons
articles.description: MIT researchers showed that the APOE4 gene variant suppresses molecular signaling needed for oligodendrocytes to myelinate neurons and also demonstrated a proof-of-concept fix.

articles.title: A soft robot could help doctors diagnose and treat disorders of the small intestine
articles.description: MIT engineers designed a robotic enteroscope that can inch through the hard-to-reach small intestine, making biopsies and drug delivery easier.

articles.title: Making machines that can listen
articles.description: Professor Paris Smaragdis develops computers with superhuman hearing for applications like speech recognition, music understanding, and environmental monitoring.

articles.title: Origami-based construction method yields lightweight, load-bearing structures on architectural scales
articles.description: The modular approach could be used to erect emergency shelters or fabricate aerospace components more quickly and with less material than some techniques.

articles.title: J-PAL North America launches Homelessness Evaluation Resource Hub to drive evidence-informed approaches to housing stability
articles.description: The hub serves as a free, online repository of essential content for policymakers, practitioners, and researchers seeking to leverage rigorous research to inform their approaches to homelessness.

articles.title: Hashim Sarkis to step down as dean of the School of Architecture and Planning
articles.description: During a dozen years of leadership, Sarkis championed projects that advanced research, education, and public engagement, and helped design thrive at MIT.

articles.title: Implantable device uses ultrasound to improve drug delivery to the brain
articles.description: This targeted approach could offer a way to prevent the recurrence of aggressive brain tumors.

articles.title: Watch the universe emerge from the dark ages, with Lumina
articles.description: The new simulation tracks dark matter, galaxies, stars, and cosmic structures over the universe’s first 2 billion years, in greater detail and volume than ever before.

articles.title: At MIT, Martha Minow speaks on sustaining democracy, both by using and overcoming AI
articles.description: In Compton Lecture, the distinguished legal scholar warns of potential “loss of the Enlightenment” while suggesting ways innovations can meet our civic and cultural needs.

articles.title: Gunter Stein, control systems and theory expert, dies at 84
articles.description: Longtime EECS adjunct professor and LIDS researcher was known for an influential essay on the need for engineers to “respect the unstable.”

articles.title: Q&A: How AI came to model the “messy” human mind
articles.description: Assistant Professor Benjamin Lindquist studies how engineers deliberately injected randomness into early AI, giving rise to deep-learning models that sometimes hallucinate.

articles.title: Persistence, teamwork, and some healthy competition
articles.description: Senior Veronica Calzadilla Sosa has taken the long route toward her MIT degree and found a supportive community along the way.

articles.title: Startup plans to rejuvenate the nuclear power industry with a new manufacturing approach
articles.description: Founded by Jake Jurewicz ’14, SM ’15, Blue Energy aims to manufacture giant pieces of nuclear reactors at shipyards and ship them on barges for final assembly.

articles.title: Tod Machover’s new symphony plays with AI while reflecting on democracy
articles.description: The MIT composer’s inventive “already and not yet,” premiering at the Boston Symphony Orchestra, uses new AI tools to create interplay with musicians while thematically exploring the fortunes of democracy.

articles.title: MIT spinout makes surgical stitching more like applying a sticky note
articles.description: SanaHeal has developed a biologically compatible adhesive that sticks to wet tissues to simplify a variety of surgeries.

articles.title: Giving AI a “crystal clear” view of the materials world
articles.description: New research can help AI models understand crystalline materials in 3D and reason about their properties.

articles.title: Fostering community amid Kendall Square’s innovation
articles.description: The 18th annual Kendall Square Association Annual Meeting explored how new technologies could be a force for shared prosperity in society.

articles.title: Satellite data reveal how Antarctica’s ice cliffs behave over time
articles.description: The cliffs don’t always collapse in the runaway process that scientists had expected.

articles.title: Q&A: The “collision” between AI, your brain, and society
articles.description: In a new book, Professor Eric So explores how the technology affects our thinking skills.

articles.title: Researchers improve weather forecasts looking two to six weeks out
articles.description: A new machine-learning approach broke records for weather forecasting for an important time frame in emergency planning.

A hidden limit of space and time could unlock electronics 100,000 times faster
articles.description: Scientists have discovered a surprising quantum limit that prevents electrons from being tracked with unlimited precision in both space and time. The breakthrough could pave the way for manipulating chemical reactions and developing electronics hundreds of thousands of times faster than today's technology.

articles.title: A nuclear blast could save Earth from an asteroid, but there's a catch
articles.description: A nuclear explosion might save Earth from a deadly asteroid, but new research suggests that hitting the wrong side could make the difference between success and disaster. Scientists found that an asteroid's irregular shape can dramatically affect how it responds to an X-ray blast, with deflection effectiveness varying nearly fivefold depending on the angle.

articles.title: Ancient Siberian tomb reveals surprising secrets of cannabis use 2,800 years ago
articles.description: Scientists investigating a 2,800-year-old Siberian tomb discovered roughly 1,000 cannabis seeds and chemical evidence suggesting ancient Scythians used the plant for its intoxicating effects. The remarkable find, surrounded by evidence of elaborate burial rituals and animal sacrifices, offers the oldest directly dated archaeological evidence of psychoactive cannabis use.

articles.title: Mysterious gas leaks suggest Mars may still be volcanically alive
articles.description: Mysterious gas emissions and fresh volcanic fissures suggest that Mars may not be geologically dead after all, with hot magma potentially still active deep underground. The discovery could point to hidden pockets of warmth and chemical energy capable of supporting microbial life beneath the Red Planet’s surface.

articles.title: Stronger flu shot linked to nearly 55% lower Alzheimer's risk
articles.description: A surprising new study suggests that a stronger flu shot could offer older adults significantly greater protection against Alzheimer's disease. Researchers at UTHealth Houston analyzed nearly 200,000 adults ages 65 and older and found that those who received a high-dose influenza vaccine had a nearly 55% lower risk of developing Alzheimer's, compared with a 40% reduction previously associated with the standard-dose vaccine.

articles.title: Don't miss: Meteor showers, fireballs, and a supermoon light up November's night sky
articles.description: November's night sky is packed with celestial wonders, from bright meteor fireballs and a close pairing of Mars and Jupiter to a spectacular supermoon. Meanwhile, NASA's Voyager 1 is making history by becoming the first spacecraft to reach a distance of one light-day from Earth.

articles.title: NASA’s Swift telescope falls to Earth after nearly 22 years in space
articles.description: After nearly 22 years of exploring the universe’s most violent explosions, NASA’s Swift Observatory has re-entered Earth’s atmosphere over Indonesia. Originally designed to last just two years, the pioneering space telescope transformed our understanding of black holes, exploding stars, and mysterious cosmic outbursts.

articles.title: Scientists just found dinosaur blood that survived 115 million years
articles.description: Scientists have discovered chemically confirmed traces of ancient blood inside 115-million-year-old dinosaur bones, challenging assumptions about how long biological molecules can survive. The extraordinary preservation could unlock new clues about dinosaur physiology and even help scientists search for ancient life elsewhere in the universe.

articles.title: An anti-aging drug may help protect the brain before Alzheimer's symptoms begin
articles.description: A surprising new study suggests that an anti-aging drug could help protect people genetically predisposed to Alzheimer's disease. Researchers found that just four weeks of low-dose rapamycin improved brain blood flow in healthy middle-aged adults carrying the high-risk APOE4 gene variant, with women showing the strongest benefits. Because declining blood flow can occur years before Alzheimer's symptoms appear, the discovery raises hopes for preventing or delaying the disease before memory loss b

articles.title: Scientists discover Europe's ancient forests were nothing like we imagined
articles.description: Scientists have uncovered evidence that Europe was dominated for more than 20 million years by open woodlands, colorful meadows, and large grazing animals, not the dense forests long considered its natural state. The surprising discovery challenges modern reforestation strategies, suggesting that planting thick forests could actually harm the biodiversity conservationists hope to protect.

articles.title: Scientists squeeze record-breaking X-ray power into an incredibly tiny spot
articles.description: Scientists have created record-breaking X-ray flashes lasting just 300 attoseconds, concentrating enormous power into an incredibly tiny spot. The breakthrough could unlock a new way to observe electrons in action and potentially control the ultrafast processes that drive chemical reactions.

articles.title: Human bodies produce 2 billion metric tons of CO2 a year just by staying alive
articles.description: Humans collectively produce more than 2 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide annually just by turning food into energy, a 74% increase over three decades largely driven by population growth. Unlike fossil fuel emissions, however, the CO2 we exhale is part of the natural carbon cycle, and scientists say measuring it more accurately could improve climate models.

articles.title: Scientists discover hidden brain changes linked to common sleep disorders
articles.description: Scientists have discovered that sleep disorders are associated with structural changes in brain regions that control attention, decision-making, and emotions, potentially explaining why disrupted sleep can affect everyday thinking and behavior. The findings, drawn from 57 brain imaging studies, reveal both shared and disorder-specific patterns that could lead to more targeted treatments.

articles.title: SLAC scientists find conclusive proof of a mysterious third type of magnetism
articles.description: For nearly 90 years, scientists believed magnetism fell into just two categories, but researchers have now confirmed a remarkable third type called altermagnetism. Using specialized X-rays, they uncovered a unique magnetic signature that proves these materials behave differently from conventional magnets. Altermagnets combine stability with the ability to efficiently carry information, potentially overcoming major limitations in today's electronics. The discovery could lead to faster computers,

articles.title: NASA is racing against time to save the Hubble Space Telescope
articles.description: NASA is exploring a daring plan to save the legendary Hubble Space Telescope from its eventual fiery plunge into Earth's atmosphere. After more than 35 years of groundbreaking discoveries, Hubble is slowly losing altitude, and without intervention, it could fall back to Earth as early as 2033 or 2034. To keep the iconic observatory operating, NASA is asking private space companies to propose innovative ways to boost Hubble into a higher orbit, upgrade its capabilities, or safely dispose of it wh

articles.title: Rubin Observatory discovers two hidden companions of the Milky Way. Hundreds more may be waiting
articles.description: The Vera C. Rubin Observatory has already uncovered two previously unknown companions of the Milky Way using preliminary observations covering just 7% of the night sky. The discoveries include an extremely faint galaxy 355,000 light-years away and a star cluster hidden behind cosmic dust. Scientists suspect hundreds of additional satellite galaxies remain undiscovered, and Rubin's powerful telescope could finally bring them into view.

articles.title: A dead star's mysterious rings reveal what could happen when our Sun dies
articles.description: Astronomers have discovered a strange double ring of planetary wreckage around a dead star, revealing a possible preview of our Solar System's distant future. The two rings are separated by a mysterious gap that researchers believe is maintained by surviving planetary bodies, including one potentially as large as Pluto or the Moon. Their different chemical compositions suggest they may contain the remains of separate destroyed planets.

articles.title: MIT scientists break a 20-year rule and unlock never-before-seen crystal structures
articles.description: MIT scientists have challenged two decades of conventional thinking by discovering that flexible molecular connections, rather than rigid ones, can unlock entirely new ways to arrange nanoparticles. The breakthrough could lead to a new generation of designer materials with unusual properties and applications in electronics, medicine, and energy.

articles.title: AI helps Stanford scientists discover a “natural Ozempic” with a surprising advantage
articles.description: Stanford researchers have discovered an AI-identified natural molecule that dramatically suppresses appetite and promotes fat loss in animals, potentially offering an Ozempic-like weight-loss treatment without common digestive side effects or significant muscle loss. Called BRP, the molecule reduced food intake by up to 50% and targets a different brain pathway, raising hopes for a more precise obesity treatment if future human trials prove successful.

articles.title: Scientists discover that a clogged filter could revolutionize oil refining
articles.description: Scientists have developed a remarkable new membrane that separates crude oil at room temperature, using the oil itself to create microscopic filtration channels. The breakthrough could cut refining energy consumption by nearly 32%, carbon emissions by almost 38%, and operating costs by 36%, potentially transforming one of the world's most energy-intensive industries.

articles.title: Scientists accidentally solve a chemistry mystery that lasted 60 years
articles.description: After more than 60 years of unsuccessful attempts, scientists have finally isolated stable examples of elusive boron-oxygen molecules once considered too unstable to capture. The surprising breakthrough, achieved using relatively simple chemical reactions, could pave the way for an entirely new class of exotic compounds.

articles.title: Five-inch-long beetle larvae are quietly destroying blueberry roots
articles.description: Scientists have solved a mystery surrounding destructive beetles attacking blueberry bushes in North Carolina, identifying a species whose massive larvae can grow up to five inches long and destroy plant roots. Although farmers have reported damage for more than a decade, the insects responsible remained unidentified until researchers used DNA analysis to uncover the culprit.

articles.title: Permanent daylight saving time has a dark side, scientists warn
articles.description: A new study warns that permanent daylight saving time could force American children to make at least 2 billion additional school commutes in darkness, potentially increasing safety risks and disrupting their biological clocks. Researchers found that fatal crashes involving school-aged pedestrians were roughly twice as likely during dark mornings as after sunrise.

articles.title: NASA smashed into an asteroid. Now Hera is closing in to see what happened
articles.description: Europe’s Hera spacecraft has captured its first clear view of two asteroids involved in NASA’s historic 2022 experiment to redirect a potentially dangerous space rock. Now approaching the pair, Hera will investigate the mysterious aftermath of the collision and uncover why the asteroid shifted far more than scientists predicted.

articles.title: A hidden star is plowing through Betelgeuse’s atmosphere, new evidence suggests
articles.description: Something mysterious is disturbing Betelgeuse, and astronomers believe they have identified the culprit: a hidden companion star called Siwarha. New radio observations reveal that the smaller star may be plowing through Betelgeuse’s enormous atmosphere, creating disturbances that subtly stretch and distort the red supergiant’s shape.

articles.title: Scientists may have finally explained why our brains and bodies are cross-wired
articles.description: Scientists propose that the brain’s mysterious cross-wiring, which connects each hemisphere to the opposite side of the body, may have originated more than 500 million years ago in the visual systems of ancient fish. Rather than evolving for a specific advantage, this unusual arrangement may simply be a legacy of evolution building new brain circuits on an ancient foundation.

articles.title: Scientists identify two overlooked skills that predict reading success
articles.description: A massive new study reveals that intelligence plays a surprisingly limited role in children's reading success, while visual processing showed no meaningful connection at all. Instead, the strongest predictors are sound recognition, vocabulary, and background knowledge, offering new clues about how to help struggling readers.

articles.title: A 50-year-old mystery of vanishing frogs reveals a hidden killer
articles.description: A nearly 50-year-old mystery involving disappearing frogs in Brazil may finally be solved, with scientists uncovering evidence that a deadly fungus swept through the region and devastated vulnerable species. Remarkably, many frog populations have since rebounded, suggesting they developed greater tolerance to the disease that once threatened their survival.

articles.title: 400,000-year-old teeth reveal a stunning twist in human evolution
articles.description: A groundbreaking discovery is rewriting the story of human evolution, revealing that an ancient human species once thought to be an evolutionary dead end may have left genetic traces in people alive today. By extracting proteins from 400,000-year-old Homo erectus teeth discovered in China, scientists uncovered evidence suggesting that these early humans interbred with Denisovans, another mysterious ancient human group. That genetic connection may have eventually reached modern populations in the

articles.title: Dead stars could break one of physics' most famous limits
articles.description: A surprising new discovery suggests that some dead stars can grow far more massive than scientists once thought possible. Computer simulations show that powerful magnetic fields could allow white dwarfs to reach 2.4 times the mass of the Sun, dramatically exceeding a famous limit that has stood for decades. The findings could help explain unusually bright supernova explosions that have long puzzled astronomers.

articles.title: The brain’s hidden fear mechanism may explain anxiety and PTSD
articles.description: A surprising new discovery suggests that fear may cause the brain to blur the line between danger and safety rather than distinguish them more clearly. By observing brain activity in mice using augmented reality, scientists found that memories of threatening and harmless environments began to overlap, potentially allowing faster responses to danger. This "better safe than sorry" survival mechanism could help explain why people with anxiety or PTSD sometimes experience intense fear in completely

articles.title: Gene editing could replace a lifetime of medication, but there's a catch
articles.description: A single gene-editing treatment could someday protect against heart disease, high cholesterol, and other common conditions for decades, potentially replacing lifelong medications. But scientists warn that permanently altering genes introduces risks that could take years to emerge, making long-term safety a critical challenge.

articles.title: Scientists turn viruses into weapons against deadly superbugs
articles.description: Scientists are advancing a promising new way to fight antibiotic-resistant infections by using viruses that specifically target and kill harmful bacteria. An international team has released the first coordinated guidelines for personalized phage therapy, offering a roadmap for safely bringing this experimental treatment into clinical practice. Early findings are encouraging, with one study reporting improvement in 77% of patients and the disappearance of targeted bacteria in 61%.

articles.title: All 5 genetic “letters” of DNA and RNA discovered in a 4.5-billion-year-old asteroid
articles.description: Scientists have discovered all five essential nucleobases used in DNA and RNA in pristine samples from asteroid Ryugu, revealing that key ingredients for life existed in space billions of years ago. The remarkable finding adds to growing evidence from other asteroids and meteorites that these molecules were widespread throughout the early Solar System.

articles.title: Scientists discover new Alzheimer’s drug that repairs DNA damage and reduces brain inflammation
articles.description: Scientists have discovered that a drug originally developed for spinal cord injuries can tackle several key features of Alzheimer’s disease, including DNA damage and inflammation. Already tested for initial safety in humans, the experimental treatment could offer a faster path toward therapies that target the disease at its roots.

articles.title: Scientists discover mysterious “lonely” brain waves linked to memory loss
articles.description: Scientists have uncovered a surprising link between Alzheimer’s-related protein buildup, disrupted brain waves during deep sleep, and fading memory. The findings suggest that hidden changes in how the brain processes memories overnight may contribute to age-related memory loss long before Alzheimer’s symptoms appear.

articles.title: Scientists solve 30-year-old mystery and discover a hidden defense against inflammation
articles.description: Scientists have solved a decades-old mystery and uncovered a hidden immune system defense that protects healthy cells from the very inflammation meant to fight infections. The surprising discovery could lead to new approaches for treating cancer, inflammatory bowel disease, and other conditions involving excessive inflammation.

articles.title: Scientists trick cancer cells into making the drugs that kill them
articles.description: Scientists have developed a promising new cancer-fighting strategy that uses carbon monoxide naturally produced by tumor cells to manufacture powerful drugs inside the cancer cells themselves. Early laboratory experiments suggest the technique could selectively attack cancer while sparing healthy cells, potentially paving the way for safer chemotherapy alternatives.

articles.title: Kids who eat more ultra-processed foods show a troubling brain response
articles.description: A new study suggests that ultra-processed foods may influence children's developing brains in ways that encourage weight gain. Researchers from USC studied 46 children ages 7 to 10 and found that those who ate more ultra-processed foods showed stronger activity in the brain's reward system when viewing tempting foods like cookies and French fries. These heightened brain responses were linked to greater increases in body fat and body mass index (BMI) one year later, suggesting that the brain's se

articles.title: A tiny squeeze dramatically changes the magnetism of exotic materials
articles.description: Scientists have discovered that a simple mechanical squeeze can dramatically alter the magnetic properties and electrical behavior of exotic materials called altermagnets. The surprising breakthrough could open the door to faster, more energy-efficient electronics and new technologies for quantum computing.

articles.title: NASA reveals a haunting skull hidden in Antarctica’s ice
articles.description: NASA satellites have captured an eerie, skull-shaped formation on a remote Antarctic island, but its haunting appearance conceals a troubling warning about melting glaciers. Unusually warm winter temperatures have exposed large areas of dark ice, potentially accelerating future melting and gradually transforming the skull's ghostly features.

articles.title: IceCube detects ghost particles with 10 billion times the energy of solar neutrinos
articles.description: Mysterious particles called neutrinos constantly stream through our bodies, and scientists are now detecting incredibly powerful versions arriving from distant cosmic sources using a massive observatory buried in Antarctic ice. These elusive “ghost particles” could hold extraordinary clues about the Big Bang, extreme cosmic events, and some of the universe’s greatest mysteries.

articles.title: Scientists just found a loophole that could let black holes split in two
articles.description: Scientists have discovered a possible loophole in the laws that normally prevent black holes from splitting apart, suggesting that extremely fast-spinning black holes might divide into two. The surprising finding raises the possibility of an entirely new black hole phenomenon that future telescopes could potentially detect.

articles.title: Large Hadron Collider reveals evidence of Big Bang matter in surprisingly small collisions
articles.description: Scientists at CERN's Large Hadron Collider have uncovered compelling new evidence that even relatively small atomic collisions can recreate the extraordinary state of matter that filled the universe moments after the Big Bang. Known as quark-gluon plasma, this exotic substance forms at temperatures more than 100,000 times hotter than the center of the Sun, causing ordinary particles to break apart into their fundamental building blocks.

articles.title: NASA's Hubble and Webb discover ancient worlds that remember their past
articles.description: NASA’s Hubble and James Webb Space Telescopes have uncovered surprising clues about the solar system’s origins by studying 27 tiny, distant objects beyond Neptune. Scientists discovered that these ancient building blocks of planets have remained remarkably unchanged for billions of years, while their unexpected sizes and numbers challenge existing theories of planet formation.

articles.title: Scientists say a forgotten particle may explain why the universe exists
articles.description: A mysterious particle overlooked for decades may hold the key to why matter survived the Big Bang, allowing stars, planets, and life to exist. Scientists believe this forgotten neutrino reshaped the early universe and may have left detectable gravitational wave signals that could help unlock the cosmos’s deepest mysteries.

articles.title: Scientists reverse liver cell aging and cut Alzheimer’s-linked protein in half
articles.description: A surprising discovery suggests that rejuvenating the liver could help protect against Alzheimer’s disease and heart disease. USC researchers found that an experimental drug restored aging liver cells in rats, cutting levels of an Alzheimer’s-linked protein in half and bringing bad cholesterol down to youthful levels. The treatment also revived a previously unknown communication system that helps liver cells remove harmful substances from the bloodstream.

articles.title: 30,000-year-old DNA reveals Ice Age Europeans were far more connected than we thought
articles.description: Scientists have uncovered surprising DNA evidence that Europeans living more than 30,000 years ago were connected across vast distances, challenging the idea that ancient populations remained largely isolated. Genetic clues from human remains and cave sediments reveal prehistoric migration, long-lasting communities, and survival through the harshest conditions of the Ice Age.

articles.title: Common pesticide linked to 2.5 times the risk of Parkinson’s disease
articles.description: A UCLA study found that long-term exposure to a common pesticide was linked to more than 2.5 times the risk of Parkinson's disease. Scientists also uncovered how the chemical damages brain cells and identified a promising way to protect them.

articles.title: Ancient ape fossil in Egypt could rewrite the story of human origins
articles.description: A 17- to 18-million-year-old ape fossil discovered in Egypt is challenging long-held beliefs about where the ancestors of humans and other modern apes first evolved. Scientists now suspect that North Africa and the Middle East, rather than East Africa, may have been the cradle of modern ape evolution.

articles.title: A mysterious 4,000-year-old wall is rewriting North Africa’s history
articles.description: A remarkable 4,000-year-old defensive structure discovered in Morocco is rewriting what scientists thought they knew about ancient North African civilizations. The massive fortifications reveal unexpectedly sophisticated prehistoric societies and suggest that the region played a much greater role in Mediterranean history than previously recognized.

articles.title: Scientists use sound waves to deliver a new attack on deadly brain cancer
articles.description: Scientists at the University of Virginia have developed a promising new strategy to fight glioblastoma, one of the deadliest and most difficult-to-treat forms of brain cancer. Their experimental approach combines focused ultrasound, tiny nanoparticles, and genetic molecules called microRNAs to attack multiple cancer-driving genes simultaneously.

articles.title: Scientists discover the hidden “muscles” trees use to straighten themselves
articles.description: Scientists have discovered that trees can sense their own shape and straighten their trunks using specialized wood that acts like opposing muscles. This remarkable ability helps trees maintain their posture and could lead to stronger forests, better timber, and more resilient crops.

articles.title: Scientists shrink Archimedes’ screw to the size of a single molecule
articles.description: Scientists have built a groundbreaking molecular motor that spins in either direction using electricity, inspired by a machine invented more than 2,000 years ago. Even more remarkably, its rotation can boost electrical conductivity by up to 100 times, potentially transforming the future of molecular electronics.

articles.title: Scientists smash oxygen nuclei to recreate matter from the Big Bang
articles.description: Scientists have recreated a primordial state of matter from the dawn of the universe by colliding oxygen nuclei at nearly the speed of light. The surprising results show that this exotic substance can form in smaller, lower-energy collisions than previously demonstrated, challenging the known boundaries of early-universe physics.

articles.title: Astronauts just gave the International Space Station a powerful upgrade
articles.description: Two astronauts completed a 7-hour, 11-minute spacewalk to install a new solar array on the International Space Station, bringing NASA one step closer to a major power upgrade. Once the final array is installed on November 5, the station will have up to 30% more available power, supporting critical operations and its eventual controlled deorbit.

articles.title: The asteroid killed the dinosaurs. Why did crocodiles survive?
articles.description: Scientists may have solved a 66-million-year-old mystery: how crocodiles survived the asteroid that wiped out the dinosaurs. A sweeping analysis of fossils and ancient climates suggests that their preference for warm environments placed them in tropical refuges that remained habitable even after the catastrophic impact.

articles.title: A simple blood test could reveal Alzheimer’s risk 10 years before symptoms
articles.description: A major international study found that a simple blood test could help predict Alzheimer’s-related cognitive decline years before symptoms appear, with the highest-risk individuals facing a 38% chance of impairment within five years and an estimated 78% chance within 10 years. Scientists believe the discovery could pave the way for earlier intervention and future treatments designed to prevent Alzheimer’s before memory problems begin.

articles.title: Scientists discover that some “unhealthy” diets can boost cancer immunotherapy in mice
articles.description: In a surprising discovery, scientists found that certain diets associated with obesity can make cancer immunotherapy more effective in mice, challenging traditional assumptions about diet and cancer treatment. The findings suggest that the secret may lie in how food interacts with gut bacteria to strengthen the immune system's response to cancer.

articles.title: Scientists discover metals that defy the deep freeze at -424°F
articles.description: Scientists have discovered a surprising mechanism that allows certain metals to resist cracking at temperatures as low as -253°C (-424°F), when similar materials typically become dangerously brittle. Instead of breaking, two experimental alloys reorganize their internal structures, creating new ways to absorb stress and remain flexible.

articles.title: Coordinated disturbances haunt grids worldwide. Here’s how researchers solved the mystery.
articles.description: Mystery solved: Coordinated power drops have been haunting power grid worldwide, but a team of researchers in Germany found the culprit.

articles.title: An ancient ocean full of giant predators reveals a surprising twist in evolution
articles.description: A remarkable fossil discovery in Colombia is challenging how scientists understand major evolutionary changes in Earth's history. Researchers uncovered an incredibly diverse ancient marine ecosystem where giant reptiles, sharks, and other creatures thrived as older evolutionary groups approached extinction and newer ones emerged. They call this previously unrecognized pattern a "Biotic Inflection," suggesting that major transformations in life can occur without mass extinctions.

articles.title: Hidden climate superpower: Why some ocean “snow” carries six times more carbon
articles.description: Scientists have discovered that the stickiness of underwater “marine snow” plays a surprisingly important role in how much carbon reaches the deep ocean. Gooier particles resist bacterial breakdown and can transport more than six times as much carbon to the depths, revealing an unexpected connection between ocean slime and Earth's climate.

articles.title: Scientists discover stunning new Amazon fish that may already be endangered
articles.description: Researchers have discovered a stunning new species of tiny orange-patterned fish in the Brazilian Amazon, but its survival may already be at risk. Named Laimosemion laranja, the brilliantly colored killifish measures less than three centimeters long and was found in just three small forest pools. Its extremely limited habitat is threatened by mining, deforestation, pollution, and expanding development.

articles.title: Einstein's equations reveal how gravity could break, reconnect, and release energy
articles.description: More than a century after Einstein revolutionized our understanding of gravity, scientists have uncovered a surprising new phenomenon hidden within his equations. Researchers at Columbia University and Universidad Adolfo Ibáñez have identified a theoretical process called "gravitational reconnection," in which structures within gravitational fields can break apart and reconnect, transferring energy into matter.

articles.title: Scientists wipe out deadly brain tumors in every mouse tested with new cancer therapy
articles.description: Scientists at UC San Francisco have developed a powerful new cancer therapy that remains inactive until it reaches the brain, where it switches on to attack deadly tumors. The engineered immune cells, called B-SYNC CAR-T cells, completely eliminated diffuse midline glioma (DMG), an aggressive childhood brain cancer that is almost always fatal within a year, in two mouse models.

NASA reveals bold new plan to return astronauts to the Moon in 2028
articles.description: NASA has revealed an accelerated plan to land astronauts on the Moon in 2028, with SpaceX and Blue Origin developing competing lunar landers and a crucial orbital test scheduled for 2027. Faster rocket preparations, new lightweight spacesuits, and redesigned missions could help pave the way for a permanent lunar presence and future human exploration of Mars.

articles.title: DNA on the Shroud of Turin reveals centuries of hidden secrets
articles.description: The Shroud of Turin, one of history's most mysterious religious artifacts, is yielding surprising new clues through DNA analysis. Scientists have uncovered a complex mixture of biological traces that may reveal more about the cloth's past and the environments it encountered. The findings offer a fresh scientific perspective on a centuries-old mystery that continues to spark fascination and debate.

articles.title: Scientists discover a surprising link between acorns and lyme disease
articles.description: After more than 35 years of research, scientists have uncovered surprising clues about what really drives Lyme disease risk. Contrary to longstanding assumptions, deer populations appear less important than mice, which can fuel a 40% increase in tick numbers the following year. Even acorn production can predict tick population surges two years in advance, while extreme temperatures may be far less deadly to ticks than scientists once believed.

articles.title: A quantum breakthrough makes light behave like both a solid and a liquid
articles.description: Scientists have observed a bizarre quantum state of matter that combines the structure of a crystal with the frictionless flow of a liquid, all at room temperature. The breakthrough overturns a major practical limitation of exotic quantum experiments and could help bring powerful new light-based computing and sensing technologies closer to reality.

articles.title: A simple supplement may help clear brain fog after cancer
articles.description: A surprising new study from UCLA suggests that a naturally occurring molecule could help breast cancer survivors overcome the frustrating brain fog and exhaustion that can linger long after treatment ends. Researchers found that women taking an oxaloacetate supplement for eight weeks experienced substantial improvements in memory, concentration, mental clarity, and fatigue.

articles.description: arXiv:2611.08626v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: E-commerce supply chains generate large volumes of customer feedback and operational data that remain underutilized in inventory management. articles.description: arXiv:2611.08647v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Intra-weight injection lets one model change another model's behaviour by editing its weights directly, without gradients. articles.title: AlterNet: Adaptive-Depth Mixture-of-Experts with Learned Halting for Elastic Inference

articles.title: AttentionSwitch: Jailbreak Defense for LLMs via Joint Learning of Sparse Attention-Head Selection and Scaling

articles.title: I Think, Therefore I Attack: Evaluating Thought Injection Attacks on Reasoning Agents

articles.title: Solver-Admitted Metamorphic Testing of Learned Network Optimization Surrogates

articles.title: Mind the Divergence: Divergence-Guided Reliability-Aware Fusion and Adaptive LLM Prompting for Conversational Emotion Recognition
articles.description: arXiv:2611.08860v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multimodal emotion recognition in conversations (MERC) integrates textual, acoustic, and visual cues to identify utterance-level emotions.
